items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Fireside chat at a Kansas City Fed economic forum in Oklahoma
items.quote: The big question now is do we stay patient?
items.summary: Reuters (published June 5, quoting remarks made Thursday June 4) reports Schmid said inflation has probably crept up into the 3.50% range and asked aloud whether the Fed should stay patient or act by raising rates a quarter point or two to 'tamp this thing down'. FXStreet's same-day report calls inflation his biggest risk.
items.score_note: Openly weighing rate increases with inflation as the main risk, but framed as a question, not a call to hike.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview at the Bloomberg Tech conference, San Francisco
items.quote: We are prepared to respond either way, whatever the economy brings
items.summary: Daly said policy is in a good place but there is too much uncertainty to say where rates are headed, and that more forward guidance could be misleading because the Fed has to wait for the economy to evolve.
items.score_note: Explicitly two-sided: ready to move either way.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Technology Summit session "Probing the Economic Impact of AI" with Caroline Hyde, San Francisco
items.quote: when we’re thinking about policy decisions, we have to think about today
items.summary: A conversation about AI and the economy. Daly said AI could be disinflationary over five to ten years but policy works on roughly a 12-month horizon, where oil prices and other shocks matter more; data-center construction has not shown up in the inflation numbers. No statement on the rate path. Time is 10:10 a.m. PT on the SF Fed page.
items.score_note: No rate-path content; the same-day TV interview carries the stance.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Banco de España conference, Santander, Spain: moderated conversation
items.quote: We continue to have policy in a slightly restrictive position, so inflation should come down
items.summary: Daly said policy is slightly restrictive so inflation should slow, and welcomed lower oil prices after the Iran ceasefire, but flagged large uncertainty. Reuters' report of the same event adds that she sees a scenario of more persistent inflation and that AI uncertainty keeps her from rushing a rate decision. Time (4:45 a.m. PT) is from the SF Fed event page, which has no transcript.
items.score_note: Hold stance: policy already slightly restrictive, next step uncertain. Torn between 0 and -1 ('restrictive enough'), chose 0 because she also raised a persistent-inflation scenario.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Kansas City Fed Economic Forum, Grand Island, Nebraska: "The Federal Reserve, Economic Outlook and Monetary Policy"
items.quote: My primary concern is inflation, which is too hot and has been above target for too long.
items.summary: Schmid said the labor market is in balance and growth is resilient, so his focus in setting policy is inflation. He argued against the textbook habit of looking through supply-shock inflation (beef, energy) and against leaning on core measures.
items.score_note: Inflation is the primary concern and he rejects looking through supply shocks, but the text does not call for a rate increase outright, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Financial Times interview (as reported by Reuters)
items.quote: earlier, incremental, gradual interest-rate action is preferable, less costly and less disruptive than potentially later, larger and abrupt actions
items.summary: Two days after the July hold, Musalem told the FT he had expressed a preference for a 25bp increase at that meeting, and that the week's Treasury selloff (30-year yield above 5.2%) showed the Fed needs to earn inflation credibility with rate increases. The St. Louis Fed lists the FT interview as July 31; the Reuters copy opened is time-stamped Aug 1 India time.
items.score_note: States he preferred a hike at the meeting just held and argues for acting earlier.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Kansas City Fed Agricultural Economic Summit, Omaha, Nebraska: "Agriculture, the Economy, and the Kansas City Fed"
items.quote: As such, I believe that bringing inflation down to the Fed’s 2 percent objective will require tighter policy.
items.summary: Speaking the week after the July FOMC, Schmid said inflation is too high, the labor market is in balance and growth is resilient. He does not see the current policy stance as restrictive and said getting inflation to 2 percent will require tighter policy. He also said the Fed should respond to aggregate inflation even when it comes from relative price rises tied to AI infrastructure demand.
items.score_note: Says policy is not restrictive and that tighter policy will be required: an explicit call for rate increases (made before the September hike).

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Q&A after the Agricultural Economic Summit speech, Omaha (same event as the 2026-08-04 speech item; split out for the AI-financing remarks)
items.quote: is that circle getting too leveraged?
items.summary: Reuters (Aug 6) reports that in his Tuesday appearance Schmid asked whether the way the AI industry finances itself is making it 'another too big to fail', and whether the circle of contractual commitments among data centers, energy providers and communities is getting too leveraged. This is a financial-stability remark, not a statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: No rate-path content in these remarks; the rate stance for this occasion is scored in the speech item of the same date.
items.ai_quote: is this industry becoming another too big to fail?

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: ESRI International Conference, Tokyo: keynote on economic shocks and monetary policy
items.quote: I was completely supportive of the decision to hold rates in July.
items.summary: Daly laid out two scenarios: a modal one where tariff, energy and AI shocks fade and mildly restrictive policy is enough, and a second where overlapping shocks compound and inflation gains momentum, which would need a more aggressive recalibration. She said the two are much closer in probability than before, backed the July hold to gather information before September, and said the Fed must be very prepared to act if the second scenario emerges. Time is 5:35 p.m. PT on the SF Fed page.
items.score_note: Supports the hold with the benign scenario still modal, but risk is one-sided toward tightening; torn between 0 and +1, chose 0.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Q&A at the ESRI International Conference, Tokyo (same event as the 2026-08-05 keynote item; split out for the AI-financing remarks)
items.quote: not of the things that happened in the financial crisis, but what could go wrong that would tip this over
items.summary: Reuters (Aug 6) reports Daly said on Wednesday that judging only by the growth rate and amount of AI investment one could call it 'very worrisome', though many commitments are still announcements rather than built assets. She said rising borrowing to fund the buildout could become an issue and the Fed should build a dashboard of what could go wrong. Not a statement on the rate path.
items.score_note: No rate-path content; the rate stance for this occasion is scored in the keynote item of the same date.
items.ai_quote: not of the things that happened in the financial crisis, but what could go wrong that would tip this over

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Centro de Debate de Políticas Públicas (CDPP), São Paulo, Brazil: "Monetary Policy and Productivity: Promoting Growth vs. Stabilizing Prices"
items.quote: it is crucial that monetary policy put a meaningful restraint on underlying inflation
items.summary: Musalem said the US economy is resilient, the labor market has stabilized, and inflation is well above 2% with risks tilted toward it staying above target for a year or more. He argued policy must restrain underlying inflation now rather than tolerate higher inflation in the hope of AI-driven productivity gains later. In the Q&A, per Reuters (kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-08-07/feds-musalem-says-central-bank-should-have-hiked-rates-last-meeting), he said he expressed a preference at the July meeting to raise the funds rate by 25 basis points.
items.score_note: The prepared text alone reads +1; the Q&A reported by Reuters (page opened) has him saying he preferred a 25bp hike at the July meeting, so +2 for the occasion.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview
items.quote: rate increases are preferable, better, less disruptive than later, potentially larger
items.summary: Musalem said policy and financial conditions are accommodative, the real funds rate is below neutral, and underlying inflation of 2.5% to 3% is too high. He confirmed he argued for a hike in July but said he keeps an open mind for the September 15-16 meeting. Full sentence in the Reuters text: 'More gradual interest rate increases are preferable, better, less disruptive than later, potentially larger, potentially more abrupt increases.' (the page has invisible characters inside it, so the quote field holds a clean fragment). The St. Louis Fed's own page for this interview is a summary without quotes.
items.score_note: Leans clearly to tightening but explicitly did not prejudge September; between +1 and +2, chose +1.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television "Surveillance" interview
items.quote: seem to be signaling to us that they understand our reaction function
items.summary: Daly said policy is in a good place and that she strongly supported the July hold. She sees no evidence of an urgent need for preemptive cuts or hikes, does not see Fed credibility at risk despite higher long-term yields, and would not prejudge how the Treasury's debt-management moves affect policy. The quoted clause refers to short-dated bonds pricing some Fed tightening.
items.score_note: Hold is appropriate, no urgency in either direction.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: CNBC "Squawk Box" interview from the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium
items.quote: I don't know what we're restricting currently with the rate policy that we're at today
items.summary: Schmid said inflation is still stubborn and sticky and that he does not see what the current policy rate (3.50% to 3.75% at the time) is restricting. He stopped short of endorsing a hike at the September 15-16 meeting, saying he needs a little more information on the demand side.
items.score_note: Policy may not be restrictive enough and inflation dominates, but he explicitly withheld a September hike call.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Bloomberg Television interview at Jackson Hole
items.quote: For me I think it might be accommodative on the short end
items.summary: In a separate Jackson Hole interview Schmid told Bloomberg TV that policy might be accommodative at the short end and added 'So we've got work to do'. Bloomberg groups him with officials who say rates are not restraining the economy.
items.score_note: Says policy may be accommodative and there is work to do; no explicit hike call in the quoted words.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Independent Community Bankers of Colorado 53rd Annual Convention, Vail, Colorado: "The Strategic Imperative of Instant Payments for Community Banks"
items.quote: With the labor market in balance and growth resilient, inflation is my primary concern as I think about the correct course for monetary policy.
items.summary: Two days after the September FOMC raised the policy rate, Schmid said he supported the decision, describing it as a response to inflation that has been too high for too long and is trending above 3 percent. He called the hike a step toward the work the Fed has to do on inflation. The rest of the speech is about instant payments.
items.score_note: Supports the hike and calls it 'a step' with inflation the primary concern, but does not explicitly ask for another increase in this text; nearer-0 choice between +1 and +2.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Reuters interview
items.quote: earlier and incremental policy firming is better and less disruptive than later and larger and potentially more abrupt policy action
items.summary: Five days after the September hike Musalem said that without further policy restraint inflation is more likely to be substantially above 2% in 18 months than at target, that inflation 'is not a risk. It's there', and that underlying inflation is moving in the wrong direction. Reuters reads this as more hikes likely needed. Interview date (Monday Sept 21) is from the Reuters URL listed by the St. Louis Fed and from Bloomberg's same-day report; the copy opened was published Sept 22-23.
items.score_note: Argues for further and earlier firming right after a hike.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: London School of Economics, Centre for Macroeconomics: speech "How and Why" and Q&A with Ricardo Reis
items.quote: My judgment is that monetary policy remains somewhat accommodative
items.summary: The prepared text (stlouisfed.org/from-the-president/remarks/2026/how-and-why-communicating-monetary-policy-framework-london) is about communicating a policy framework and has no stance on the next move. Bloomberg reports that after the speech he said policy remains somewhat accommodative even after the September hike and that central bankers may need to rethink looking through supply shocks; Bloomberg characterizes this as reiterating that more hikes are likely needed.
items.score_note: The direct quote only says policy is still accommodative; the 'more hikes needed' wording is the reporter's, so +1 rather than +2.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: 2026 Community Banking Research Conference, St. Louis: introductory remarks (introducing Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman)
items.quote: we are proud to once again host the annual Community Banking Research Conference, now in its 14th year
items.summary: Welcoming remarks about the conference and the Fed, CSBS and FDIC partnership. No monetary-policy content.
items.score_note: No policy content; included for coverage audit.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Axios interview
items.quote: I was very pleased, very supportive of the rate hike we took in September
items.summary: Daly called the September hike completely necessary given higher inflation risks. Whether more is needed depends on whether the tariff, oil and AI shocks fade (she still puts some probability on not needing more) or compound and last longer. She said AI demand is spreading beyond high-end chips and relief is further out than usual, and that hyperscalers are not very rate-sensitive though tighter policy still affects the inflation outlook.
items.score_note: Backs the hike and leaves the door open to more, conditional on shocks; she gives only 'some probability' to being done, so a tightening lean rather than neutral.
items.ai_quote: These hyperscalers aren't very interest rate-sensitive

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Bloomberg "The Future of Fixed Income" event, New York: moderated Q&A
items.quote: bring inflation back to target in a timely manner, more monetary
items.summary: Reuters reports Musalem said the Fed will need to hike again: 'To bring inflation back to target in a timely manner, more monetary policy firming will be required' (the page has invisible characters inside the sentence, so the quote field holds a clean fragment). On the late-October meeting he said he goes in with a very open mind and has not prejudged it. The St. Louis Fed's own page for the event is a summary without quotes.
items.score_note: Unhedged statement that more firming will be required, though no commitment on the October meeting.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Reuters interview (day of the September CPI release)
items.quote: We are more likely than not to need additional adjustments, but the timing of those adjustments to me is something we’re still deliberating
items.summary: Daly said further rate increases are more likely than not but she feels no urgency to decide at the October 27-28 meeting on limited information. She said the CPI report shows inflation risk remains elevated, that reacting to risk when there is time is imprudent, and that markets understand the Fed's reaction function.
items.score_note: Expects more hikes but explicitly not urgent; between +1 and +2, chose +1.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Shadow Open Market Committee meeting, New York: keynote "Remarks on the U.S. Economy and Monetary Policy" and Q&A with Jeff Lacker
items.quote: I judge that additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon.
items.summary: Two days after the October hold, Musalem said policy and financial conditions remain accommodative and that further firming will be needed soon, preferring earlier small steps over larger abrupt moves later. His more likely scenario has inflation staying meaningfully above 2% without more tightening; a less likely one has it falling on its own (energy, productivity, or an AI/data-center spending slowdown). He noted credit spreads have widened, especially for AI-infrastructure borrowers, but is not overly concerned by tighter financial conditions.
items.score_note: Explicitly says additional firming is necessary and soon.
items.ai_quote: Credit spreads in cyclical sectors and for high-yield borrowers have widened, especially for those borrowers involved in the AI infrastructure build.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Greater St. Louis Inc. event, Saint Louis Art Museum: speech "Your Fed: Decentralized by Design" and Q&A with John Kemper
items.quote: must return inflation to 2% on a timely basis
items.summary: The prepared text (stlouisfed.org/from-the-president/remarks/2026/your-fed-decentralized-by-design) is about the Fed's regional structure and independence and has no rate content. In the Q&A, per FXStreet, he said people remain concerned about inflation at the current level, expectations are anchored, and the Fed must return inflation to 2% on a timely basis, attributing excess inflation to energy shocks and the AI buildout.
items.score_note: Inflation-first message; no explicit rate call in the words quoted for this event.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: CNBC "The Exchange" interview with Steve Liesman (day of the October jobs report)
items.quote: My expectation is we’re going to have to tighten policy further.
items.summary: Daly said she expects further tightening, with timing and size still to be decided, and that she is prepared to do more if the economy calls for it. She described households as on a treadmill of high inflation after almost six years above target, and said the volatile backdrop, including the painful but orderly repricing of tech stocks, argues for being deliberate and gradual. Interview date is from the CNBC video URL listed by the SF Fed; the article opened is dated Nov 9.
items.score_note: Expects more tightening but stresses gradual and undecided timing; between +1 and +2, chose +1.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Energy conference hosted by the Kansas City Fed and Dallas Fed, Houston
items.quote: We've got to continue to focus on that demand and make good policy decisions to equalize what's happening between inflation and labor.
items.summary: Dow Jones reports Schmid called the benchmark rate 'fairly accommodative' and said there is still a lot of underlying demand, with inflation top of mind while employment is steady. The report says he views the rate as still too loose and reads his remarks as part of a chorus pointing to hikes.
items.score_note: Calls policy fairly accommodative with demand strong; the hike implication is the reporter's framing, so +1 not +2.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: "Balancing the Stack: Affordable Housing Finance Forum", Kansas City Fed, Kansas City, Missouri: "Housing Costs: Challenges and Opportunities"
items.quote: our price-stability mandate requires that we set the policy rate to control economy-wide inflation rather than favor one sector over others
items.summary: A housing-supply speech. On rates, Schmid said the Fed cannot set the policy rate to help housing, and that long-term rates have risen much more than the policy rate, largely for reasons beyond monetary policy such as the surge in AI investment pulling in global capital. No statement on the next policy move.
items.score_note: No rate-path guidance; he only declines to ease for housing's sake. Torn between 0 and +1 (mild pushback on lower rates), chose 0.
items.ai_quote: Much of the recent increase in longer-term interest rates appears to reflect factors beyond monetary policy, such as the extraordinary expansion of investment in artificial intelligence.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR) Fall Policy Forum "Economic Policy in the Age of AI": keynote and conversation with Neale Mahoney
items.quote: my bias is that further tightening will be needed
items.summary: Daly said the Fed has an inflation problem (above target for six years, moving in the wrong direction) alongside a stable labor market and good growth. She was comfortable with the September hike and has a bias toward further tightening, but said how much and when need not be decided today, and that tighter financial conditions are welcome and aligned with where policy needs to be. AI is not the main inflation driver but adds pressure; investors re-pricing the risk of AI firms' borrowing strategies is healthy. Time is 10:10 a.m. PT on the SF Fed page.
items.score_note: Tightening bias stated, but she says timing and size are open and markets are doing some of the work; between +1 and +2, chose +1.
items.ai_quote: the borrowing strategy, et cetera, is going to be as risk-free as it seemed earlier on, or are we going to price in a little more risk?

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: UNLV Center for Business and Economic Research Economic Forecast, Henderson, Nevada: moderated conversation
items.quote: We're going to need to, in all likelihood, raise rates
items.summary: Daly said her bias is that the policy rate will need to rise and that she will deliberate it with colleagues in December and at later meetings. She cited services inflation excluding housing moving the wrong way and producers running out of room to absorb costs in margins, and is watching whether resilient consumer spending holds through the holidays. Reuters notes she did not comment on the timing of hikes. Time (9:00 a.m. PT) is from the SF Fed event page, which has no transcript.
items.score_note: 'In all likelihood' raise rates and mentions December, but hedged and no timing commitment; between +1 and +2, chose +1.

items.speaker: Jeffrey Schmid
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: National Credit Union Management Association 2026 Conference, Kohala Coast, Hawai'i: "The Economic Outlook, Monetary Policy and Payments"
items.quote: The Fed does have the tools to address inflation and has the responsibility to achieve price stability.
items.summary: Schmid said inflation is running too hot (PCE 3.6 percent, three-month CPI at a 5.7 percent annualized rate) and moving in the wrong direction, while the labor market is in balance. He rejected two narratives: that inflation is only supply shocks the Fed cannot offset, and that AI-driven demand is immune to higher rates. He echoed Warsh that the Fed has work to do. The date comes from the Kansas City Fed speeches listing and sitemap; the page itself shows no date.
items.score_note: Clear inflation-first lean and 'we have work to do', but no explicit sentence asking for a hike at a given meeting; nearer-0 choice between +1 and +2.
items.ai_quote: The AI buildout is often central to this narrative, with the argument that AI investment will continue apace even if confronted with higher interest rates.

items.speaker: Alberto Musalem
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (non-voter 2026)
items.occasion: Central Bank of Argentina 2026 Money and Banking Conference, Buenos Aires: "Remarks on the U.S. Economy and Monetary Policy" and Q&A
items.quote: I judge that further removal of monetary policy accommodation will be necessary soon.
items.summary: Musalem said the economy will likely need several rate increases before spring 2027, with the real policy rate moving from the low end of 1% to 1.5% today to solidly between 2% and 2.5%, and that the nominal rate may have to do most of the work. He said policy and financial conditions are still tailwinds and not yet restraining inflation. An unlikely alternative scenario (lower energy prices, productivity, or an AI/data-center spending slowdown) would need no further firming.
items.score_note: Explicit call for several rate increases, starting soon.
items.ai_quote: Credit spreads in cyclical sectors and for high-yield borrowers have widened, especially for those borrowers involved in the AI infrastructure build.

items.speaker: Mary Daly
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (non-voter 2026, voter 2027)
items.occasion: Virtual conversation at a St. Louis Fed conference (day the October FOMC minutes were released)
items.quote: This measured approach we've been taking, and I would be supportive of continuing to take, is the right way to go
items.summary: Stocktwits reports Daly said further rate increases will be required to return inflation to 2% but favored a measured pace, citing uncertainty over tariffs, the Iran conflict and AI capital spending. The article contrasts her with Waller's call for a 50bp move in December.
items.score_note: More hikes needed per the report, but the direct quote argues for a measured pace and against larger moves; +1.

coverage_notes: Presidents confirmed on each bank's own site in this session: Alberto Musalem (stlouisfed.org/from-the-president), Jeffrey Schmid (kansascityfed.org/speeches), Mary Daly (frbsf.org events pages). No successor to cover. Official lists used: St. Louis Fed 'Remarks and Speeches' (every entry from June 1 to Nov 17 checked), Kansas City Fed sitemap of /speeches/ (Schmid entries July 16, Aug 4, Sept 18, Nov 12, Nov 15), SF Fed events and news-coverage lists via the site API. Thin months: Musalem June (the St. Louis Fed lists only two district visits, June 1 and 5, no remarks) and July (FT interview only); Schmid June (one fireside chat), October (only headline-level wire reports, kept in unverified); Daly September (nothing found on the SF Fed lists or in wire searches) and late June. Skipped as non-policy: Musalem's Oct 14 Open Vault Q&A on the Fed's structure (read, no rate stance) and SF Fed operations stories. Reuters.com, Bloomberg.com, NYTimes.com, CNBC video pages and the Post-Dispatch copy could not be read directly, so interviews are sourced to syndicated copies (Kitco, Devdiscourse, The Star, Bloomberg Government, Morningstar/Dow Jones, MPA, FXStreet, Stocktwits) that carry direct quotations. Several Reuters reprints embed zero-width characters inside sentences; quotes were cut to spans free of them, so two quotes are fragments (Musalem Aug 20 and Oct 8) with the full sentence given in summary. kansascityfed.org and stlouisfed.org timed out for command-line fetches from this PC and were read in a browser; their quotes were checked by exact substring match there, all other quotes against saved page text. Two same-event Q&A segments (Schmid Aug 4, Daly Aug 5) are split into separate null-scored items so the AI-financing quotes sit with a page that contains them; do not count them as extra occasions. ai_financing was also tagged where a speaker tied the rate path or long rates to AI investment and its funding (Schmid Nov 12 and Nov 15, Musalem Oct 30 and Nov 17 on credit spreads, Daly Oct 6 and Nov 12); Schmid Nov 15 is the loosest of these. Context check: pages opened agree with the brief (July hold with three hike dissents, 25bp hike on Sept 16 to 3.75-4.00%, October hold, December hike priced). Musalem and Schmid both said they favored a hike at the July meeting as non-voters. One Reuters item says Musalem votes in 2027; not checked further.
